title: Complementarity constraints as nonlinear equations: Theory and numerical experience
contribution: Shows that MPCCs can be solved by SQP after replacing complementarity with any of a family of NCP functions (including three new exact smoothings of the min/natural-residual function) without a smoothing parameter, proves KKT/strong-stationarity equivalence and superlinear local convergence, and ranks the formulations on MacMPEC (read from ANL/MCS-P1054-0603 preprint).
problem_entry: Received verdict that MPCCs as NLPs are 'numerically unsafe' because X1x2<=0 violates MFCQ everywhere (p. 2); asks which NCP-function reformulations work without the smoothing parameter of [8,10] (p. 3).
key_idea: Replace complementarity by x1,x2>=0, Phi(x1,x2)<=0 with an NCP function, fix the subgradient convention grad phi(0,0)=0 so KKT points equal strongly stationary points, relax the linearization by delta*min(1,phi)^(1+kappa), omit grad^2 Phi from the QP Hessian; algorithm unchanged (pp. 3, 9, 13).
assumptions: [A0]-[A5] (convention, C2 Lipschitz, MPCC-LICQ, MPCC-SOSC, nonzero multipliers, independent QP basis) p. 14; [A6] exact complementarity p. 15; [A7] consistent QPs, called 'clearly an undesirable assumption' p. 18; linear complementarity only p. 23; A2/A3 flagged most restrictive p. 14.
proof_devices: Min-function linearizations consistent near strong stationarity under MPCC-MFCQ = CQ-like property, Prop. 3.6 (p. 11)
Common gradient structure tau_a, tau_b unifies all NCP functions; Thm. 3.7 KKT <=> strong stationarity with multiplier maps (pp. 11-12)
Basic/minimum-norm multiplier of the multiplier ray (3.8) (p. 12)
Equivalence of QPs to relaxed-NLP QPs when complementarity holds, Lemmas 5.3-5.5, Thm. 5.6 (pp. 15-17)
Basis-by-basis reduced NLPs with LICQ+SOSC, Lemmas 5.7-5.10 (pp. 19-21)
Finite number of bases => superlinear convergence, Thm. 5.12 (p. 22)
Filter outcomes (A)/(B)/(C) used to predict behaviour (p. 13)
experiments: MacMPEC (~150, some 32x32 discretizations dropped with stated bias, p. 23); 8 formulations in his SQP-filter solver via AMPL interface; untuned defaults (p. 24); iteration and CPU performance plots with failures set large (p. 25); failure list by mode TR too small / infeasible QP / iter. limit (p. 26); failures tied to non-strongly-stationary problems, IEEE errors excluded as model errors (p. 27); xi as strong-stationarity indicator; per-instance appendices (pp. 30-36).
positioning: Extends own [17]; contrasts with smoothing NCP methods [8,10] ('smoothing is not required', p. 3); credits Anitescu elastic mode and IPM relaxations as parallel routes; calls the pessimistic verdict 'premature' (p. 2).
writing: One-sentence contribution (p. 3) restated in conclusions (p. 28); plain negative reporting ('disappointing', p. 27); hedged open questions ('At present, we believe', p. 29); a Discussion of Proofs section giving geometric intuition (pp. 22-23).
limits_future: Global convergence from remote starts and avoiding C-stationary limits open (p. 29); nonlinear complementarity not covered (p. 23); no quadratic rate with kappa<1 (p. 14); proposes lumped NCP formulation e'Phi<=0 (p. 29).

title: Solving multi-leader–common-follower games
contribution: Characterizes EPEC (multi-leader-common-follower) solution sets as intersections of simpler Nash games and derives NCP, MPEC and NLP formulations from concatenated strong-stationarity conditions plus a square price-consistent NCP, solving the whole EPEC as one problem and publishing the MacEPEC test set (read from ANL/MCS-P1243-0405 preprint).
problem_entry: Electricity-market EPECs solved by cyclic diagonalization or Su's sequential smoothed NCP; entry is the MPEC-as-NLP lesson applied to all leaders simultaneously (p. 4).
key_idea: Strong stationarity of each leader's MPEC = KKT of its NLP reformulation; concatenate them into a nonsquare NCP (4.1), remove degeneracy with basic-multiplier complementarities (4.4), give MPEC (min l1 of xi) and penalized NLP versions, and a price-consistency restriction that yields square NCPs for PATH (pp. 12-20).
assumptions: Followers convex with CQ ('We accept these limitations', p. 6); MPEC-LICQ for each leader (Prop. 4.1, p. 14); [A1] 'not very restrictive', [A2] 'rather restrictive' (pp. 17-18); electricity models violate [A2] (p. 25).
proof_devices: Solution set = intersection of k generalized Nash games, Thm. 3.1 (p. 10)
Equilibrium => strongly stationary via Scheel-Scholtes under MPEC-LICQ, Prop. 4.1 (p. 14)
Local solutions of (4.6)/(4.7 with zero penalty) are strongly stationary, Thm. 4.1 (p. 16)
Complete separability => equivalence with a single collective-loss MPEC, Prop. 5.1 (p. 21)
Two-player parametric example mapping zero/one/infinite price-consistent equilibria (pp. 21-22)
experiments: New MacEPEC library: 30 random QPEC-leader EPECs (single-precision data to increase degeneracy), academic ex-001/example-4/outrata3-4, three electricity models incl. 14-node PJM (pp. 22-25); every formulation as separate AMPL file; baselines GJ, GS, NCP(t) reimplemented; filterMPEC and PATH; iteration counts (CPU avoided, reason given); tags [I], [S], CYCLE; solution comparison across solvers (pp. 26-29).
positioning: Builds on Pang-Fukushima EPEC paradigm and Su's strong-stationarity definition; 'In contrast, we attack (4.1) directly' vs Su's smoothing (p. 12); diagonalization and special-purpose MPEC methods require more work (p. 7).
writing: Calibrated: 'no clear overall winner' (p. 28), 'competitive' in conclusions (pp. 29-30); admits baseline-only success on electric-1 (p. 28); first-person acceptance of limitations (p. 6).
limits_future: No MPEC solver guarantees strongly stationary limits; how to formulate/presolve NCPs, MPECs, EPECs to expose structure such as skew symmetry (p. 28, p. 30); hand-coding strong-stationarity conditions is error prone (p. 25).

title: FilMINT: An outer approximation-based solver for convex mixed-integer nonlinear programs
contribution: Implements Quesada-Grossmann LP/NLP-based branch and bound inside MINTO with filterSQP, shows by one-feature-at-a-time ablation which MILP techniques carry over to convex MINLP, and introduces cut-style management of ECP/fixfrac/NLPR linearizations, giving a solver competitive with Bonmin (read from ANL/MCS-P1374-0906 preprint; appendix not in file).
problem_entry: Aim of MINLP at a small multiple of MILP cost (p. 4); old thesis observation that simplistic LP/NLP-BB beat NLP-BB and OA by an order of magnitude, yet no implementation besides concurrent Bonmin (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Build LP/NLP-BB entirely in MINTO user callbacks (no core changes) with warm-started filterSQP and its restoration phase, and treat linearizations as MILP cuts: violated-only, cut pool, depth-biased probability min{beta 2^-d,1}, tailing-off, per-node caps, hierarchy ECP < fixfrac < NLPR (pp. 9, 18-24).
assumptions: Convex twice-differentiable f, g; compact polyhedral X, Y (p. 4); heuristic use for nonconvex (p. 4); finite OA convergence cited 'under mild conditions' (p. 7); dual preprocessing invalid for OA master (p. 13).
experiments: 222 convex instances (MINLPLib, MacMINLP, CMU-IBM) converted to AMPL; tiers by MINLP-BB time (100 easy dropped, 37 moderate, 85 hard); 4 h limit; time profiles for moderate, scaled solution value for hard (pp. 10-11); ablation ladder vanilla -> single MILP features -> vanIP -> row-mgmt -> linearization schemes -> filmint (pp. 11-25); final vs MINLP-BB and two dated Bonmin versions; 88/122 solved (p. 27); defaults tuned on all previous experiments (p. 27).
positioning: Credits Quesada-Grossmann ('clever extension of outer approximation', p. 5) and Leyffer 1993 thesis; four explicit differences from Bonmin (p. 5); Linderoth-Savelsbergh 1999 for branching expectations (p. 16).
writing: Mostly calibrated ('not competitive ... for difficult instances' p. 11; strong branching 'surprising' p. 16; 'Further research ... will be required' p. 23) with one strong claim ('conclusively demonstrates', p. 25); abstract stronger than the Bonmin-v2 tie in Section 4 (p. 3 vs p. 27).
limits_future: Convex only (p. 4); future heuristics and cutting planes (p. 27), better point selection (p. 23), Benders aggregation deferred (pp. 20-21); unstated: tuning on comparison suite (p. 27), easy tier dropped (p. 11).

quotes.text: Our aim is to provide a solver that is capable of solving MINLPs at a cost that is a small multiple of the cost of a comparable mixed integer linear program (MILP).
a fundamental design philosophy is to treat linearizations of the nonlinear feasible region in a manner similar to the way cutting planes are treated by a branch-and-cut algorithm for MILP.
